CHAPTER XVI

THE PRESS (1868)

At ten o'clock of a July night, in heat that made the tropical rain-shower simmer, the Adams and Motley families climbed from their Cunarder to a government tug and were set ashore in blackness at a North River pier. They felt as Tyrian traders might have felt, stranger on a shore changed past knowing in ten years. The Dutch historian turned diplomat and the private secretary turned private citizen hunted carriages to the Brevoort House, and towards midnight took shelter in their native land.

How far it had changed they could only guess. America groped, like an earthworm, to catch up with its head and find its tail, its few score leaders stretched far ahead of millions of immigrants, negroes, and Indians lingering in archaic time. For the moment all seemed to move one way, which gave America a vast advantage over Europe’s cross-purposes; but if Europe or Asia once polarized, the lead might vanish. Each newcomer must slip as near the head of the caravan as possible, and first of all learn where the leaders were.

Power lay plain enough: coal, iron, steam had taken command over agriculture, handwork, and learning. For a survivor of the fifties the change worked like the earthworm’s motion; he twisted in vain to recover his trail; he had become estray, flotsam, a belated reveller, a scholar-gipsy like Matthew Arnold’s. His world was dead. Not a Polish Jew fresh from the Ghetto, snarling weird Yiddish at the customs officers, but had keener instinct and freer hand than he—American of Americans, backed by Puritans and Patriots and a civil-war education. He made no complaint; Indians and buffalo had been ejected by his own people; but he insisted the fault was not his. Unfairly forced from the track, he must get back as best he could.

He had one comfort: his father and Motley were even less fitted for the new work. All were survivals from the forties—bric-à-brac of Louis Philippe’s day; stylists, doctrinaires, ornamental odds and ends with little value in Desbrosses Street or Fifth Avenue. The men who earned high pay were not ornamental, and the country needed energy and capital more than ornament. To fit out a continent with roads and decencies would exhaust the world’s credit. The mere suggestion of a sun is an outrage to a deep-sea fish that carries a lantern on the end of its nose; from the coming of railways, life took on extravagance.

The belated reveller at Desbrosses Street spent his force seeing his own length. The new Americans must create their world—a science, society, philosophy, universe—before they had created roads or dug their iron. They had no time for thought; their attitude to the universe was that of the deep-sea fish. Above all, they disliked being told how to do their work by men with abstract theories. They knew their world was one of new energies. The more one knew, the less one was educated.

Society had been forced to waste energy on settling what should never have been revived, and by sheer force broke resistance down, leaving only the fact of power. Then it threw itself on roads. The fraction called the railway system mortgaged the generation between 1865 and 1895; no one knew it better than the generation itself.

Whether or not he knew it, Henry Adams acted as if he did. Back in Quincy, his brother Charles struck for the railroads; Henry for the press; they hoped to play into each other’s hands. They found no one else to play with. After discovering the worthlessness of a so-called education, they found as much in so-called social connection. With all his acquaintance, no one could help him. He was for sale in the open market, and cheap. The want of solidarity between old and young seemed American; the young must impose themselves as a necessity and compel purchase. He sometimes thought he was expected to blackmail. The labor market of good society was ill-organized.

Boston offered no market for educated labor. Changed as it was, it perplexed more than ever. He needed above all the press, but meddling with the Boston press was worse than useless; so with politics. Boston meant business. The Bostonians were building railways; he would have liked to help, but had no education for it. Newport was charming, but it gave no education; society assumed all was for the best New Yorkers in the best of Newports, and that all young people were rich if they could waltz: a new Ant and Grasshopper. After three months the only man who spoke for him was Edward Atkinson. Beacon Street might be as good as any, and the path from Beacon to State Street and back might be surest; who could tell? Temperament aside, neither temperament nor education fitted him for Boston. He had reckoned on outlawry as his birthright. The mere thought of Mount Vernon Street lowered his pulse.

He stuck to the press and chose Washington as the shortest road to New York. In 1868 Washington stood outside the social pale; a Bostonian going there announced himself an adventurer and office-seeker. The risk was great, the more because he had no clear plan but to educate himself over again in hostile air. Money did not trouble him; what troubled him was finding a press. The North American Review was not a press; the Nation would give him letters; he needed a New York daily and none needed him. The death of Henry J. Raymond lost him his one chance. The Tribune was impossible; the Sun required a dash of blackguardism he could never keep up; the Herald admitted no personality but Bennett’s. The Holy Land of the Evening Post and the New Jerusalem of the Nation were open, and reached the same circle as the North American Review. The outlook was dim, but it was all he had.

Here Mr. Evarts helped as Boston had not. He had the social instinct of the man-of-the-world, generous, prodigal, fond of youth, accepting the world without scolding it. In October, 1868, he took Adams to Washington, and Adams gratefully took a sleeper that made him doubt the value—to him—of a Pullman civilization, and took shelter in Evarts’s house at H and Fourteenth till he found rooms in the roomless village. To him it seemed unchanged: few houses, fewer rooms, the same men; comforts needless; his best chance still lay in the eighteenth century.

The first acquaintance was naturally the President. Evarts presented him to Andrew Johnson, whose stock remark was that the young man looked even younger than he was. Adams felt younger still. He never saw Johnson again, but the figure stayed: the old-fashioned Southern Senator, lifted by moral certainty of rightness. The Southerner could not doubt; that self-assurance made Johnson a true President. Looking back, Adams thought the Executive in 1868 perhaps the strongest he was ever to see.

Seward was still Secretary of State, little changed yet somehow closed with the public; he no longer cared, asked, or gave. Adams often went of an evening to his whist, and when the end drew near, asked him to dine and play in his rooms. Seward came, played, and, in parting, said only: “A very sensible entertainment!” It was the single favor Adams ever asked or took. So, as teacher after twenty years, Seward passed; and the Treasury took the State Department’s place in Adams’s interest.

The Secretary of the Treasury, Hugh McCulloch, seemed a stop-gap rather than a force; a banker in a bankers’ world, which Adams instinctively distrusted; yet McCulloch proved the broadest, most liberal, most genial, and most practical public man in Washington. The financial system was chaos; reform pressed everywhere; no one knew how well McCulloch did till his successor tried to better him. Officials dread interference; every friend in power is a friend lost; apparent exceptions are rare, and McCulloch was one. Without past or future, he could afford company. His rooms filled with active, eager young men—volunteer types greedy for reform, ready for a fight, unselfish and, by the measure of youth, honest. The whole government needed reconstruction as much as in 1789; the finances were a scandal; the tariff worse; and McCulloch faced reform with large good-nature, outside parties and jobs.

Chaos bred life; the army bred courage. Adams liked being one of them, felt at home in the Treasury, and fancied he and his friends owned this administration, which, in its dying days, had neither friends nor future except in them.

Just then the Supreme Court was to take up the Legal Tender cases. Evarts, anxious to face Judge Curtis, forced discussion, wanting an anvil to hammer his ideas on. Adams, flattered to be an anvil, contradicted with freedom; the question was more historical than legal. Seeking light for his letters and articles, he went to the Chief Justice himself. Mr. Chase, one of the old Free Soil leaders, had been author of Legal Tender as Secretary and became its enemy as Chief Justice; he loved power as though still a Senator. He was willing to gain an ally who would tell his story as he wished; intimacy in his house helped the comforts of a newspaper adventurer.

Sooner or later he must meet Charles Sumner. On the street they met, and Sumner, after surprise, dropped at once into the old relation of hero to school-boy, which Adams amusedly accepted at thirty to Sumner’s fifty-seven. The renewal bristled with thorns, but it interested him as a study. Sumner asked nothing of Adams’s people or past; he talked only of the present, and treated Adams almost confidentially, inviting him to his pleasant little dinners on La Fayette Square and into his study. Adams liked and admired him, and thought his mind a pathological study—the calm of water which receives and reflects images without absorbing them. If a disagreeable image ruffled it, it rejected as mechanically as it had admitted. Not more egoistic than some, he was so wholly so that the disease affected the whole mind. For a newspaperman he was the more useful.

In 1868 the authorities who were the stock-in-trade of the newspaper business—capital hoarded from a Silurian age—still stood about La Fayette Square. Within a few hundred yards of the nursery monument to Andrew Jackson, society, hotels, banks, markets, and government were gathered; beyond the Square the country began. No rich stranger, no idle man of letters or science, no artist or gentleman without office had yet made a home there. It was rural and primitive; scarcely a soul had known life in a great city; the happy village had no club; a one-horse tram on F Street sufficed; the State Department lodged in an infant asylum far out Fourteenth Street while another architectural infant asylum rose by the White House; real estate had not risen since 1800; pavements were worse than the mud. In four-and-twenty hours one knew everybody; in two days everybody knew one.

After seven years’ vain effort to explore London’s outskirts, Washington gave easy repose. From Evarts’s roof he looked on the men he was to work with—or against—and admitted that nine-tenths of his education was useless, the tenth harmful. He must begin again; learn to talk to the Western Congressman and hide his antecedents. The task amused him. The lobby was picturesque; society gave freely what it had; politics, for the moment, lay in tidal slack-water; and the Government resembled Henry Adams in education: all that had gone before was useless, and some of it worse.
